title: AI in the Classroom: New Report Highlights What Parents Want
author: Jared Hayden, Ken Burchfiel and Michael Toscano
summary: This Institute for Family Studies piece summarises a new survey report on what parents of K-12 students want from AI in schools, arguing that while administrators push AI, parents have not been consulted. Nearly four in ten students already attend schools where AI use is allowed or required, and only 15% attend schools that block it. Yet 56% of parents want AI fully blocked and another 26% want less of it, while only 13% want more. The most popular model is a "computer lab" where AI is used in discrete classes and the rest of schooling is books and handwriting, and more than two in three parents want AI introduced in high school or later, or never. Large majorities believe AI will undermine learning (77%), enable malicious behaviour (79%) and expose children to serious risks (73%), and 75% of Republican and 72% of Democratic parents support pausing AI in schools, as New York City and Los Angeles have done.
points: Parents have largely not been asked about AI in schools, and the report fills that gap with national survey data.
A majority of parents want AI blocked entirely and few want it widely used, even as many students already attend schools that permit or require it.
The most favoured arrangement is confining AI to computer labs while keeping books and handwriting central.
Parents want AI later in a child's schooling, with only 3% supporting use in kindergarten.
Opposition is bipartisan: three quarters of Republican parents and nearly as many Democrats support pausing AI in classrooms.
quotes: Over the past decade, as new research exposed the deleterious effects of digital technologies on children’s health and development, a growing movement of parents has objected to the ways in which social media and screens are transforming childhood.
Naturally, the move to limit digital technology in childhood has also led parents to scrutinize educational technology, or “ed tech,” and, ultimately, rethink screen-based education altogether.

Nearly 4 in 10 American students in primary or secondary education attend schools where AI use is either explicitly allowed or even required. By contrast, 15% of American students attend schools where the use of AI in the classroom is officially blocked.
The current trajectory—AI grouped with tablets as the basis of education—is very unpopular with most parents. Only 11% of parents want this form of education for their kids.

The numbers rise in middle school and high school (21% and 25%, respectively), but nearly as many want it introduced in 12th grade or later (20%) or not at all (22%). In sum, parents as a group are generally not eager to have AI introduced in schools at any specific stage, though later years score modestly better.

As for benefits, only 46% agree that AI will help children learn by personalizing their learning experience, and a mere 39% say it will boost childhood creativity. The most popular positive case for AI in schools is that it will prepare children for the workforce of the future (51%).
But that’s not what we found. In fact, 75% of Republican parents support the policy to pause AI in schools, as do 72% of Democratic parents.
